Community Health Advisory: Lung Cancer Prevention and Early Detection

Lung cancer forms in the cells that line the airways of the lungs, and anyone can develop the disease. The leading cause and biggest risk factor is smoking tobacco, with the risk rising the longer and more frequently an individual smokes. Non-smokers are also placed at risk through secondhand smoke exposure. Other critical risk factors include being over 70 years of age, past radiation therapy to the chest, family genetics, and exposure to environmental carcinogens such as radon, asbestos, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, chromium, nickel, coal smoke, soot, silica, diesel fumes, and particulate air pollution. 

For prevention, individuals who do not smoke should avoid starting, while current smokers are strongly urged to quit, as quitting reduces the likelihood of new lung tumors developing. Healthcare providers can assist with cessation counseling and medications, and patients can ask about clinical trials studying chemopreventive agents.

The goal of lung cancer screening is early detection before any symptoms appear, which is when treatment is most successful and can help prevent death. Screening is not recommended for everyone, but rather is intended for people assessed as being at high risk based on their individual risk factors and family medical history. Community members should consult their healthcare providers to determine whether they qualify for screening. 

Regarding symptom awareness, lung cancer is frequently diagnosed only after symptoms appear or when routine blood tests turn up abnormal findings. Symptoms vary depending on where a tumor grows or spreads, and tumors can prevent the lungs from getting necessary air. Additionally, some individuals may develop symptoms stemming from paraneoplastic syndromes, which are abnormal bodily responses triggered by the cancer. Anyone experiencing concerning changes or who may be at elevated risk should promptly consult their medical care team.
prediction.ground_truth:
Community Health Advisory: Preventing and Detecting Lung Cancer Early

Lung cancer is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths, with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) being the most common type. The primary risk factor for lung cancer is tobacco smoking, but exposure to secondhand smoke, radon, asbestos, air pollution, and certain occupational hazards (such as diesel fumes) also increase risk. While anyone can develop lung cancer, individuals with a history of heavy smoking or significant exposure to these risk factors are at higher risk and should discuss lung cancer screening with their healthcare provider. Screening, such as low-dose CT scans, is recommended for those at high risk and can detect lung cancer at an early, more treatable stage—often before symptoms appear. Early symptoms may include a persistent cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, or unexplained weight loss. Quitting smoking and minimizing exposure to harmful substances are the most effective ways to reduce your risk. Regular checkups, updating your healthcare provider on your family and exposure history, and being aware of new or persistent respiratory symptoms are important for early detection. Participation in clinical trials and supportive care services may also improve outcomes for those diagnosed with lung cancer.
